summary.traveler: Singapore has no restrictions on the import or export of foreign currency. However, travellers carrying SGD 20,000 or more in cash — in Singapore or foreign currency, or both combined — must declare this to the Immigration and Checkpoints Authority (ICA) or Singapore Customs upon arrival or departure. This is a declaration requirement under the Corruption, Drug Trafficking and Other Serious Crimes (Confiscation of Benefits) Act, not a restriction on carrying amounts.
summary.business: Singapore operates with a fully open capital account and no exchange controls. It is a leading international financial centre. Businesses may freely hold, invoice, and settle in foreign currencies. Financial institutions are regulated by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS). No capital controls apply. AML and CFT obligations apply under the Corruption, Drug Trafficking and Other Serious Crimes (Confiscation of Benefits) Act and the MAS Notice on Prevention of Money Laundering.

rules.bring_foreign_currency_in: There are no restrictions on the amount of physical currency or bearer negotiable instruments (CBNI) that may be brought into Singapore. However, any traveller carrying SGD 20,000 or more in combined physical currency and CBNI must submit an electronic Cash Movement Report (Form NP 727) via the ICA website or MyICA app within 72 hours before arrival. As of 13 May 2024, paper forms at checkpoints are no longer accepted. CBNI includes bills of exchange, cheques payable to Cash, promissory notes, bearer bonds, money orders, and postal orders. The reporting obligation applies to individuals, couriers, and recipients of mailed or shipped cash. Failure to declare is an offence under the CDSA. This is a transparency and AML measure, not a currency control. Source: ica.gov.sg/enter-transit-depart/at-our-checkpoints/for-travellers/CBNI.
rules.take_foreign_currency_out: There are no restrictions on the amount of foreign currency that may be taken out of Singapore. The same SGD 20,000 declaration threshold applies at departure. Travellers must declare to Singapore Customs if they are carrying SGD 20,000 or more in physical currency. This is purely a transparency and AML measure and does not restrict the right to carry or transfer amounts above the threshold.
rules.cash_declaration_threshold: The cash declaration threshold in Singapore is SGD 20,000, covering physical currency (coins and printed money) and cash-like bearer negotiable instruments (CBNI) — including bills of exchange, cheques payable to Cash, promissory notes, bearer bonds, money orders, and postal orders. The combined value of currency and CBNI must be declared if it exceeds SGD 20,000 or the equivalent in foreign currency. Since 13 May 2024, declaration is mandatory in electronic form only via Form NP 727, submitted through the ICA website or the MyICA mobile app (iOS/Android). Paper forms at the airport are no longer accepted. Declarations can be submitted within 72 hours before arrival or departure. Failure to declare or submitting an inaccurate report is an offence under Section 60(1) of the Corruption, Drug Trafficking and Other Serious Crimes (Confiscation of Benefits) Act 1992 (CDSA). Penalties: fine up to SGD 50,000, or imprisonment up to 3 years, or both; cash may also be seized. Source: ICA (ica.gov.sg/CBNI); SPF (police.gov.sg/STRO).
rules.resident_holding_rules: Singapore residents may freely hold foreign currency accounts domestically and abroad. There are no restrictions on the amount of foreign currency that residents may hold, purchase, convert, or transfer. Singapore's fully open capital account and its position as a global financial centre means foreign currency banking services are widely available in all major currencies. No reporting obligations equivalent to the US FBAR apply for foreign accounts under Singapore law.
rules.non_resident_rules: Non-residents may freely hold bank accounts in Singapore in SGD and foreign currencies. No restrictions apply to capital repatriation. Non-resident investors may freely transfer profits, dividends, and capital. Singapore's regulatory framework is designed to attract international capital flows. All transactions are subject to AML and CFT compliance under MAS regulations.
rules.business_invoicing_settlement: Singapore businesses may freely invoice, settle, and hold balances in any currency. No mandatory conversion requirements exist. Singapore is a major foreign exchange trading centre, with a deep and liquid FX market. All licensed financial institutions, including banks, payment service providers, and currency exchange businesses, are regulated by MAS. AML and CFT obligations apply under MAS Notices on Prevention of Money Laundering and Countering Terrorism Financing.
rules.exchange_controls: Singapore maintains a fully open capital account with no exchange controls. The Singapore dollar is freely convertible. The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) manages the SGD through an exchange rate-based monetary policy centred on the Singapore Dollar Nominal Effective Exchange Rate (SGD NEER), but does not restrict currency movements. Singapore is the world's third-largest FX trading centre by volume. No capital controls apply to inflows or outflows.
rules.banking_conversion_practicality: Foreign currency exchange is extremely well-developed in Singapore. Licensed money changers, banks, and online FX platforms offer competitive rates. ATMs accepting international cards are ubiquitous. The banking system is supervised by MAS and is among the world's most sophisticated. Singapore's Clearing House Interbank Payments System (CHIPS equivalent) and FAST payment system facilitate rapid domestic and international transfers. Foreign currency accounts in USD, EUR, GBP, AUD, JPY, HKD, and other currencies are standard offerings.
